messages.author: dbc6143acd666a4e
messages.subject: Raster process
parts:
G'day all,

Normally if I was using NicheMapR I'd set my locations of interest (often cell centroids) into a data table or data frame, one row per location, and then just loop through each location and run the model out that way, parallelizing the hell out of it if needs be. For one of the projects that I'm playing with now I've just got too many locations to model, and that approach might take me 15 months or more.

I have been learning how to use rasters as a more efficient way of analysing stuff generally, and all my data are now set up and stored as rasters, but I can't figure out a way of applying micro_global (and all things downstream) to a raster brick in a meaningful way. I figure that somebody has done this before, because I've seen some pretty big data sets produced. Anybody have any tips?

Cheers

Sean Tomlinson

messages.author: dbc6143acd666a4e
messages.subject: Re: Raster process
parts:
G'day Mike,

Thanks for getting back to me. That becomes a bit of a question of cost/benefit doesn't it? Invest the time and maybe make it quicker, or just plod along with what I know works, but might take a full year or more of processing.

One last question for you, just to confirm my thinking or otherwise, do you think it would be a more rapid process if it was working with rasterised data? I'm kind of new to the world of rasters, and I understand that they store data more efficiently, but I'm not at all sure if that means that the calculations turn over more rapidly. If not, it's really hardly worth the effort.

Cheers

Sean

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: Raster process
parts:
Hi Sean,

Not sure but there will be precedents out there I'm sure. I guess the other question is, do you really need to do that many calcs to answer your question? And could you do enough calculations that you have a set of points that you could statistically interpolate with confidence to a higher resolution? E.g. along the lines of:

Carter Anna L., Kearney Michael R., Hartley Stephen, Porter W. P., & Nelson Nicola J. (2018). Geostatistical interpolation can reliably extend coverage of a very high-resolution model of temperature-dependent sex determination. Journal of Biogeography, 45(3), 652–663. doi:10.1111/jbi.13152

All the best,
Mike

messages.author: dbc6143acd666a4e
messages.subject: Re: Raster process
parts:
G'day Mike,

The high number of points is kind of unavoidable, because the focus is trying to couple edaphic data to physiological performance of strongly range-restricted plants. So these plants occur in tiny (4-45 km2) distributions on individual ridges, and even there they choose pockets on the ridges. Resolution matters in understanding where they might be, and we have pretty decent resolution in some edaphic models. We're now trying to see whether we can estimate some microclimate parameters that might make a sensible link between the local habitat and the plant physiology that we have measured at different sites.

You're right, though. If we can interpolate accurately, we don't need to calculate everything. I'll take a look at that.

Cheers

Sean

messages.author: 606bdb90568efad9
messages.subject: Re: Raster process
parts:
Hi Sean,

This won't help you much with explicit modelling of physiological performance, but as a starting point for the microclimate, it might be worth taking a look at the integration of microclima and NicheMapR Mike and I put together last year: 

https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13330

The microclima package takes rasters of e.g. terrain as inputs and gives you hourly gridded outputs, using NicheMapR to do some of the microclimate model calibration.

Cheers,

Ilya

messages.author: dbc6143acd666a4e
messages.subject: Re: Raster process
parts:
G'day Ilya,

Thanks for getting back to me with this. It's an interesting idea. For this project I'm already a quarter of the way through developing the layer for the downscaling solution the Mike suggested, so I'll just knock that one over by plodding right along I think. I have other projects where generating raster grids right off the bat is going to be easier though.

I have a couple of questions about it: First, what does it do in regards to processing time? Presumably you can chunk the process so that it runs over a subset of pixels or a subset of the extent rather than just turning it over and twiddling your thumbs until the RAM cache is full?

Second, if the microclima package spits out hourly gridded outputs, then you should be able to stack these and maybe introduce them to the ectotherm algorithm as "micro" in a similar way to how it's sometimes done in a parallelized loop. I take it that you guys didn't try that yet? I know that Mike's opinion is that you'd need to restructure how NicheMapR does its thing, but it might go easier on the memory if that works. Like I said, I've got another project where this might be useful, so if you guys haven't tried it I'll let you know how I go

Cheers

Sean

messages.author: 606bdb90568efad9
messages.subject: Re: Raster process
parts:
Hi Sean,

You set the extent and duration by giving the run function a raster of elevations and start and end dates, so can chunk it that way (e.g. by chunking your study area). 

It returns a 3D array of microclimate values for each grid cell & hour, so easy to then feed stuff into the ectotherm model point by point quite easily.

What I am not sure is if it returns everything you need for the ectotherm model, but there are fairly easy workarounds for that (or easy tweaks I could make to the package) - feel free to contact direct about this. 

Cheers,

Ilya
